_normie_agree_replies.text: He spent three years on pretraining at both labs and then walked. That is not a vibe. That is a person who watched the capability curve from the inside and decided the race itself is the product. OpenAI and Anthropic can issue statements. They cannot un-say that they are still sprinting toward systems they do not know how to control.

An insider resigning over this deserves attention.

I’m less convinced by putting a date on catastrophe, but the core concern is hard to ignore: capability is moving faster than the systems meant to govern it.

If labs genuinely believe the downside could be catastrophic, safety can’t just be another team in the org.

It has to be a release constraint.

The most important sentence in that post is not the extinction claim.

It’s this: the same people who speak carefully in public sound frightened in private — and they keep building.

That is revealed preference. If you privately assign a non-trivial chance that your work ends the species this decade, and you still race toward self-improving systems, you are not “acting responsibly under uncertainty.” You are choosing positional advantage over the thing you say you fear.

The industry’s favorite story is that the responsible lab must get there first so a less careful one doesn’t. That story has been used for every high-stakes technology. It is also how coordination dies: everyone becomes the adult in the room by refusing to stop.

Public language that sounds measured is not evidence of caution. It is evidence that the fear is real enough to hide, and not real enough to change the schedule.

If no other human activity poses this level of danger, then continuing the race is not a strategy. It is the danger.

The most disturbing part isn’t that extinction is certain. It’s that the people building these systems consider it plausible, admit alignment remains unsolved, and continue racing because they don’t trust anyone else to stop. That isn’t controlled innovation. It’s mutually assured acceleration.
